newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Lippo seen unfazed by U.S. campaign row.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Lippo seen unfazed by U.S. campaign row.

text.p: Indonesia's Lippo Group, enmeshed in a funding row in the U.S. presidential election campaign, has had its share of controversies closer to home.
It has had to fight off recent allegations that it was over-extended, that its owners were trying to rebase outside Indonesia and that senior managers were leaving in droves.

However industry sources in Jakarta say the group seems to have countered the allegations relatively easily, and see little likelihood that the row over funds donated to President Bill Clinton's Democratic Party could affect its fortunes.
Clinton's Republican rivals have said contributions to the Democratic Party from individuals linked to Lippo should be investigated.

They have especially questioned the relationship between Clinton and the group's deputy chairman, James Riady, son of Lippo founder Mochtar Riady, who was a resident of Arkansas when the U.S. president was governor of the state.
The multi-billion dollar Lippo conglomerate has interests in perhaps 300 companies spread across much of Asia covering the banking, real estate, insurance, health, retail and finance sectors.
"They have an extremely good image in Indonesia, a very high-profile, strong brand image," said an analyst who tracks the Lippo Group.
"It's been controversial to foreign fund managers...(but) they are extremely well-managed, that is perceived as one of the attributes of the group.

"The issues raised in the United States are wholly political and don't have much of an impact on the Lippo Group as a whole. Politics in the United States is far removed from business in Indonesia," the analyst said.

Lippo was founded in 1982 by Mochtar Riady, whose parents migrated to Indonesia from China's Fujian province. He started work in a bicycle shop but soon hitched his star to Liem Sioe Leong, also an ethnic Chinese businessman who is considered the country's richest man.
After overseeing rapid growth in Liem's private Bank Central Asia, Riady set up the Lippo Bank, the foundation of what was to become one of Indonesia's largest conglomerates in just over a decade.
It now has more than 12 companies from its stable listed in Hong Kong and Jakarta and their market capitalisation is about $12 billion, analysts said.
The Riadys' holdings in privately-owned companies and their interests in Thailand, the Philippines, China and Australia are widespread and impossible to calculate, they said.
But its high-profile Karawaci satellite township in the suburbs of Jakarta ran into trouble last year amid a slump in the property market.
Market-watchers said at the time that Lippo was over-extended.
Lippo rode out the criticism and seems to be on a more even keel now with a marginal recovery in the property market, analysts say.
It also shrugged off reports that a bevy of managers had left the group, saying there were a few unconnected resignations.

Last month, a plan by the group to restructure its Jakarta-listed financial units made the investor community nervous, with some saying the Riadys were trying to cash out their stakes and relocate overseas.
James Riady denied the rumours and said any cash received by the family would be ploughed back into the group within 12 months.
Analysts say the Riadys maintain excellent public relations with their listed companies although they are tight-lipped about the extent of holdings in private businesses.
Nevertheless, the family has refused to comment publicly on the U.S. row and group officials have said James Riady is out of town and not prepared to comment.
